<description>
A mistake here would be critical, as it would allow a malicious peer to stall us indefinitely for free. This is not currently an issue because:
- while on Linux accepted sockets do not inherit O_NONBLOCK, we always send() and recv() on Linux/macOS/BSD with MSG_DONTWAIT;
- while on Windows MSG_DONTWAIT is unset, accepted sockets do inherit the non-blocking option [^1].

Therefore, set accepted sockets (inbound P2P connections and HTTP clients) as non-blocking explicitly, like CreateSockOS() does for the sockets it creates. A belt-and-suspenders check costs virtually nothing here, and we already have similar ones for less important options (such as TCP_NODELAY, which as far as i know is inherited by accepted sockets on all our supported platforms).

[^1]: Source is [this](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winsock2/nf-winsock2-accept#remarks) implicit remark in the accept() doc, plus my own testing.
</description>

Reviewed the HTTP, P2P, and I2P paths and they look OK.

The option is set before the socket is handed to the event loop. If setting it fails, the connection is rejected, and ownership remains safe on every return path.

This change removes reliance on inheritance (which doesn't work on Linux as explained) or per-call `MSG_DONTWAIT`, and is therefore a worthwhile defense for our socket threads.

There are no tests here (nor would I expect there to be), so I had a clanker write up a small Python socket probe for Linux to verify (my) kernel's behaviour against what we are relying on here:

1. A socket accepted from a nonblocking listener did not inherit `O_NONBLOCK`.
2. `recv(..., MSG_DONTWAIT)` on that otherwise-blocking socket raised `BlockingIOError` instead of blocking.
3. Setting `O_NONBLOCK` with `F_GETFL`/`F_SETFL` succeeded and the flag could be read back.
4. After setting it, plain `recv(..., 0)` raised `BlockingIOError` instead of blocking.

All behaved as expected.
